text: Drying and storage of rice (ការហាល/សម្ងួត និងការរក្សាទុកស្រូវ) matter because grain that stays wet after threshing develops mold, discoloration, insects, and quality loss. Sun-drying (ការហាលស្រូវ) is realistic for most smallholders: spread paddy in a thin, even layer on a clean mat, tarpaulin, or concrete surface (never directly on contaminated soil), turn periodically for even drying, and protect it promptly if rain arrives. This is hardest during the wet season (រដូវវស្សា) and its transition, when cloudy weather and sudden rain interrupt drying; the dry season (រដូវប្រាំង) makes drying easier but farmers should still avoid excessive/rapid drying that increases grain cracking. A moisture meter (ឧបករណ៍វាស់សំណើម) is preferable when available since appearance and touch are unreliable, but do not hard-code one universal moisture percentage -- the right target depends on storage duration, grain/variety, and local recommendations. After drying, store paddy clean, dry, and off the ground, protected from rain, rodents, insects, birds, and livestock. Low-cost smallholder improvements: clean the storage area first, repair rodent entry points, keep bags off the floor and away from walls where possible, don't mix newly harvested grain with older grain, and inspect regularly for insects, condensation, mold, unusual odors, or localized warming -- investigate immediately rather than waiting. If sun-drying is repeatedly interrupted by rain or the farmer has too much grain to dry safely, ask whether a nearby rice mill, trader, or cooperative offers shared mechanical drying rather than assuming the farmer must own a dryer. The core rule: dry first, store second -- never put wet paddy directly into storage bags.
